exercises.title: Dialogue works the same
exercises.body: Shavian borrows all of English punctuation unchanged — quotes, commas, question marks, full stops. So dialogue reads exactly as you would expect: {{“𐑣𐑧𐑤𐑴,” 𐑕𐑧𐑛 ·𐑕𐑨𐑥.}} That says: “Hello,” said Sam.

exercises.caption: Sound it out — what does this say?
Sound it out — what does this say?

exercises.title: Two speakers, two lines
exercises.body: On the page a conversation is just alternating quoted lines, exactly as in English. Read this one as two voices: {{“𐑸 𐑿 𐑮𐑧𐑛𐑦?” 𐑭𐑕𐑒𐑑 ·𐑕𐑨𐑥. “𐑯𐑪𐑑 𐑘𐑧𐑑,” 𐑕𐑧𐑛 ·𐑥𐑧𐑜.}} The naming dot marks who is speaking, since there are no capitals to do it.

exercises.caption: Write out the reply in English

exercises.title: Questions
exercises.body: Question words are old friends by now — 𐑢𐑪𐑑 what, 𐑢𐑺 where, 𐑣𐑵 who — and a question mark does the rest: {{𐑢𐑺 𐑦𐑟 𐑞 𐑛𐑪𐑜?}}

exercises.caption: Read the question, then write it out in English

exercises.title: The small courtesies
exercises.body: The politest words in English are also among the shortest in Shavian, and you can already read every letter in them. {{“𐑔𐑨𐑙𐑒 𐑿,” 𐑕𐑧𐑛 ·𐑚𐑧𐑯. “𐑲 𐑨𐑥 𐑕𐑪𐑮𐑦,” 𐑕𐑧𐑛 ·𐑥𐑧𐑜.}} Notice 𐑔 doing quiet work at the front of thank — the whispered th, not the buzzing one.

exercises.caption: Sound it out — what does this say?
Sound it out — what does this say?

exercises.title: said, says, asked
exercises.body: Watch the vowels: said 𐑕𐑧𐑛 and says 𐑕𐑧𐑟 both rhyme with bed — English spelling hides that, Shavian doesn’t. asked is 𐑭𐑕𐑒𐑑, with the long 𐑭 of standard British speech. (Accents vary; printed Shavian usually follows one standard voice.)
